additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional Disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent, non-bizarre or less clearly bizarre delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thinking, or marked mood episodes that would suggest schizophrenia or a mood disorder with psychotic features. Outside of the delusional beliefs, overall functioning is often relatively preserved, and behavior may appear largely appropriate, which can delay recognition and treatment. The content of the delusions is typically systematized and circumscribed (e.g., persecutory, jealous, somatic, grandiose, or erotomanic themes), and individuals may seek legal, medical, or interpersonal “solutions” to issues stemming from the fixed beliefs. The course is usually chronic, with limited insight and resistance to contradictory evidence, and it is differentiated from obsessive-compulsive or overvalued ideas by the degree of conviction and imperviousness to reasoning.

patient.personality: Justin is a visionary yet somewhat disorganized IT leader who combines technical curiosity, artistic sensibility, and a generally relaxed, mentoring style with a tendency to get absorbed in his interests.
patient.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Justin’s company underwent a major restructuring that placed him under a new, more controlling executive who questioned several of his long-standing infrastructure decisions and hinted that his team might be outsourced. For someone who had built his identity around being a trusted, forward-thinking IT architect and mentor, this felt like a deep professional invalidation, especially as budget cuts delayed projects he believed were essential and sidelined him from strategic meetings. He began to ruminate extensively, alone in his office and on long hikes, poring over system logs, emails, and casual remarks from colleagues in an effort to make sense of what he saw as a pattern of targeted undermining, gradually organizing these interpretations into a rigid explanatory framework that he shared only with his wife and a few close coworkers. Over the following 14 months, his insistence on this explanation increasingly strained relationships at work and at home, and when his wife noticed he was turning down community mentoring events and spending evenings gathering “evidence” instead of playing guitar or gardening, she encouraged him—along with HR’s suggestion after a tense meeting—to seek a psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’m here because I have these beliefs about what’s going on around me, and no matter what anyone says, I just can’t shake them.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: For over a year now I’ve been completely convinced that the new exec and a couple of people in security are quietly building a case to push me out—like when I see certain log entries get altered after I flag them, or notice them stop talking when I walk into a meeting, it just fits too perfectly with this pattern I’ve mapped out in my notes, and no matter how many times my wife or HR say it’s all coincidence, I just can’t see it any other way.
